questions.q: Why isn't plain linear regression a good fit for a yes/no target?
options: It can't be trained on binary data at all
Its outputs can fall outside 0 to 1, so they aren't valid probabilities
questions.explain: A straight line can output values like 1.4 or -0.3. Logistic regression passes the linear score through the sigmoid so outputs stay between 0 and 1.

questions.q: What does the sigmoid function do?
options: Squashes any real number into the range 0 to 1
Splits data into train and test
questions.explain: The sigmoid, 1 / (1 + e^-score), maps any score to a value between 0 and 1, which can be read as a probability.

questions.q: clf.predict_proba([[6]]) returns [[0.15, 0.85]] for a churn model. What does it mean?
options: There is an 85% chance the customer stays
The customer is 6 months from churning
There is an 85% predicted probability of churn and 15% of staying
questions.explain: The columns follow the class order: first the probability of class 0 (stayed), then class 1 (churned). Here that is 15% and 85%.

questions.q: A coefficient of -0.107 gives e^-0.107 of about 0.90. How should this be read?
options: Each extra month cuts the churn probability by exactly 10 percentage points
Each extra month multiplies the odds of churning by about 0.90, holding other features fixed
questions.explain: Exponentiating a logistic coefficient gives an odds ratio. It changes the odds of the positive class, not the probability by a fixed number of points.

questions.q: How can you make a churn model catch more actual churners, accepting more false alarms?
questions.explain: Lowering the threshold labels more customers as churners, which catches more real churners but also flags more customers who would have stayed.
